The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s failure to ensure the proper preflight assembly of the glider's wing attachment system, which resulted in substantial damage to the wing structure during flight.
t:
The pilot reported that he and three club members assembled the glider before the accidewnt flight, following the manufacturer's assembly procedures. After a preflight inspection and positive control check, the glider was towed and released. Approximately 10 minutes later, the pilot heard a sharp cracking sound and elected to return to the airport and land. A postflight examination revealed substantial damage to the wing spar root, wing, and fuselage.
During disassembly of the glider following the accident, the assembly crew noted that the right main wing pin was in its halfway position and had not been secured. The left main wing pin was fully inserted and secured. They noted that the in-flight structural damage was likely due to the right main wing pin not being fully seated and secured during assembly.

cause: The pilot’s improper approach, which resulted in a faster than normal touchdown and subsequent runway overrun.
t:
The pilot reported that during his first landing attempt at the back-country airport, the airplane was too high on the approach, so he performed a go-around. He flew a longer final approach to prepare for the second landing attempt. After touchdown, the airplane was traveling too fast to stop before the end of the runway. The pilot said he “pulled up” to avoid vehicles parked at the departure end of the runway; however, the airplane did not attain sufficient altitude to clear the obstacles. The nose landing gear and lower fuselage struck an unoccupied parked vehicle, and the left wing subsequently struck a signpost. The airplane rotated about 180° and came to rest about 200 ft beyond the end of the runway. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. The pilot sustained a minor injury, and the passenger sustained a serious injury.

The pilot further stated that he likely encountered a tailwind during the landing attempt. He noted that the density altitude and tight canyon operating environment were not familiar to him; that he did not verify the airplane’s ground speed using the on-board GPS on the downwind and final legs. The pilot added that had he done so, he might have recognized the problem earlier. He stated that he had previously reviewed the Idaho Department of Aeronautics operating procedures document. Based on that information, he determined that once he had touched down on the runway he was committed to the landing, and a go-around was not advisable.

The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s failure to extend the landing gear prior to landing.
t:
The pilot reported that, while performing a straight-in approach to land, she forgot to extend the landing gear and landed the airplane with the landing gear retracted. She stated that during the approach, she did not make her usual verbal callout of “gear/flaps” and did not utilize the airplane’s written checklist. She heard the audible warning horn for the landing gear prior to landing but was unfamiliar with the annunciation at the time. The airplane touched down on the runway with the gear retracted and slid to a stop, resulting in substantial damage to the lower fuselage. 
The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

On June 6, 2026, at 0900 central daylight time, an Aero Commander, N27007, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident in Fabens, Texas. The private pilot received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot stated that the engine run-up prior to takeoff and the subsequent takeoff roll were normal. About 30 seconds after liftoff, he noticed that the airplane was unable to maintain a climb rate, and the airspeed was quickly decreasing. He then reduced the airplane pitch attitude. While the airplane was about 300 to 500 ft above the ground, he verified that the throttle, mixture, and propeller controls were fully forward, and the auxiliary fuel pump was still. He located a field to attempt a forced landing and then extended the landing gear. During the forced landing to a field, the airplane touched down hard, which resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage, wings, and empennage.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

cause: The pilot’s failure to extend the landing gear before landing.
t: The pilot reported that, during a straight-in approach, he forgot to extend the airplane’s landing gear and that he landed with the landing gear retracted. The airplane slid to a stop on the runway and sustained substantial damage to the lower fuselage. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The loss of engine power due to fuel starvation. Contributing to the accident was the separated wing fuel tank screen and sealant debris in the fuel tank.
t:
While returning to the departure airfield after completing an aerial application, the engine lost power and the pilot conducted a forced landing to a field due to insufficient altitude to attempt an engine restart. During the forced landing, the airplane struck trees resulting in substantial damage to the right wing and fuselage. 
Postaccident examination of the airplane by company personnel revealed that the right-wing fuel screen was not attached and fuel tank sealant debris obstructed the fuel tank outlet port. The pilot reported that the accident could have been prevented by ensuring that all fuel screens are in place each season and removing any loose fuel tank sealant.

cause: The pilot’s failure to maintain control of the airplane during an aborted landing attempt which resulted in an aerodynamic stall.
t: The pilot and the pilot-rated passenger were on a personal cross-country flight and upon reaching their destination, the pilot wanted to perform some practice landings. During the first landing attempt, she was too high on approach and performed a go-around. During the second attempt, the pilot stated that while attempting to land, after touchdown, the airplane turned to the right. She used left brake and rudder to attempt to regain directional control and applied engine power to abort the landing. Several eyewitnesses reported that the airplane appeared to bounce twice after landing, after which they heard the engine power up before the left wing dropped, impacted the turf runway, and “tumbled” before the airplane came to rest. The impact resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. Postaccident examination of the airplane’s flight controls revealed no evidence of any preimpact failures or anomalies that would have precluded normal operation. Given this information, it is likely that during the aborted landing attempt, the airplane exceeded the critical angle of attack resulting in an aerodynamic stall.

On June 11, 2026, about 1030 eastern daylight time, a Cirrus SR20 airplane, N858SD, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Wheelers Mill, Ohio. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Airport surveillance video captured the pilot refueling his airplane before the accident flight. Fuel receipts gathered from the fixed-based operator revealed that he added a total of 20 gallons of 100 LL fuel from the airport self-service pump. The video then showed the pilot complete his preflight inspection, start the airplane’s engine, and taxi the airplane to the runway hold short line. About 3 1/2 minutes later, the video showed the airplane depart from runway 18. The video captured the airplane’s takeoff and initial climb. The airplane briefly left the video frame before it is seen in a near vertical descent, rotating about its longitudinal axis, before an impact with terrain.
A witness observed the takeoff sequence and stated that the airplane sounded normal. He stated that he saw the airplane bank to the left before it was obscured by a tree line, followed by a loud bang and visible smoke plume.
The wreckage came to rest upright after impacting the garage of a residential home. There were no ground injuries. The airplane and residential home were destroyed by the postimpact fire (see figure 1). The Cirrus Airframe Parachute System (CAPS) rocket, lanyard, and collar were found about 165 ft northwest of the main wreckage; the CAPS parachute was observed aft of the horizontal stabilizer, partially extracted.

Figure 1. Overview of accident site.
No mechanical anomalies were found with the airframe or the engine during the onsite examination that would have precluded normal operations. The airplane was recovered from the accident site and transported to a secure location.

cause: The pin on the nose gear brace assembly that engages with the cam on the nose landing gear door actuator shaft was not seated inside the cam, which rendered the nose landing gear inoperative.
t:
The pilot reported that upon entering the traffic pattern, he lowered the landing gear. He heard a loud “bang,” and only the main landing gear position indicator lights illuminated. The pilot contacted a friend on the ground to confirm if all three landing gear were down. The friend reported that the main landing gear were down. However, the nose gear was not down, and the nose gear door was closed. The pilot departed the traffic pattern and went through the emergency gear extension procedure. The nose landing gear position indicator light would still not illuminate. The pilot made the decision to perform a gear-up landing. The panels on the belly of the airplane were substantially damaged.
A postaccident examination revealed that the pin on the nose gear brace assembly that engages with the cam on the nose landing gear door actuator shaft was not seated inside the cam, which rendered the nose landing gear inoperative. According to the airframe manufacturer, the pin is only in the slot when the landing gear door is retracted. The pin can disengage from the cam if there is a rigging issue and the rods for the door actuator are adjusted incorrectly or if the door actuator operating spring breaks. 
The mechanic who performed the last annual inspection reported that he utilized the approved airframe manufacturer maintenance manual for gear inspection and testing. According to the mechanic, the landing gear and gear door rigging were all within tolerance of the tensions and clearances called out in the maintenance manual, so no adjustments were made. He also confirmed that he examined the door actuator operating spring postaccident, and it was not broken.

a: Burkhart Grob Flugzeugbau G103 TWIN ASTIR
cause: The flight instructor’s improper planning during the simulated aborted launch which resulted in a touchdown on unsuitable terrain.
t:
The flight instructor reported that while practicing an immediate landing after liftoff, with the student pilot at the flight controls, the glider landed past the end of the runway in tall grass on a downward sloping hill. The left wing lowered and the glider pivoted and came to rest in a muddy area. The rudder sustained substantial damage during the landing. The flight instructor reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the glider that would have precluded normal operation. 
The flight instructor remarked that in the future he would plan to terminate the tow earlier so there would be sufficient runway remaining to land on and brief whether the terrain beyond the runway was suitable for landings.

a: Airborne Windsports Pty Ltd EDGE XT-912-L
t:
On June 25, 2026, about 2000 central daylight time, an Airborne Windsports Pty Ltd Edge Xt-912-L weight-shift-control light sport aircraft, N912CV was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident at Winona Municipal Airport (ONA) Winona, Minnesota. The pilot was fatally injured. The aircraft was operated under Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 as a personal flight.
Before the flight, the pilot removed the Streak 3 king post wing that was on the aircraft for 2 years and installed an Arrow strutted wing. According to his friend, who witnessed the accident, the wing was replaced just before the accident flight, and the purpose of the flight was to test the new wing. The pilot replaced the wing because the strutted wing had a lower height clearance and made it easier to store the aircraft in the hangar. A second friend, who helped with the installation of the wing, said that they made sure that the wing was properly attached before the test flight.
According to the friend who witnessed the accident, the pilot performed 2 “crow hops,” in the aircraft by taking off on runway 30 and immediately landing again on the runway before taking off a third time to fly the traffic pattern. The witness said that the “crow hops” and traffic pattern were unremarkable until the aircraft turned onto final approach. When the aircraft was on final approach, it looked like the pilot made a small correction and then banked to the left followed by a hard 90° bank to the right. The right wingtip impacted the ground first and the aircraft tumbled. The witness said that due to his location on the ground, he could not hear the aircraft engine, but he could see that the propeller was turning before and during the accident sequence.
The wreckage came to rest about 140 ft north of runway 30. Initial impact was marked by a ground scar followed by a second ground scar about 3 ft southeast. Initial impact to the main wreckage was about 15 ft long. The debris path consisted of the right main landing gear and bits of blue plastic from the wheel fairings. The main wreckage came to rest inverted and consisted of the pilot and passenger pod, wing, left main landing gear, nose gear, engine, and 3-blade composite propeller. The wing was torn and folded in the direction of travel. The tips of the propeller blades were shorn off. The structural tubing was bent and/or broken. Two cables attached to the right side of the wing batten were broken and had a broom straw appearance. The fuel selector was in the “off” position because it was turned off by first responders. The ignition was in the “on” position. There was nothing found during the postaccident examination of the aircraft that would have precluded normal operation.
According to the airframe logbook, the last annual inspection was performed in April 2024. A review of the pilot’s logbook revealed that the pilot had a total of 223 aircraft hours, 114 of which were in weight-shift-controlled aircraft. The pilot was

On June 26, 2026, about 1045 eastern daylight time, a Boeing/Jones 75, N3993C, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Cleveland, Georgia. The pilot and passenger sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. 

The pilot reported that the accident flight was the first flight after an annual inspection was completed on the airplane on May 11, 2026. During the initial climb after takeoff, just above the trees, the climb performance degraded and the airplane could not gain altitude, as if the engine was not developing full power. The pilot then initiated a slow, right turn in an attempt to return to the airport; however, he observed that he did not have enough altitude to clear obstacles back to the airport and elected to perform a forced landing in a cornfield. During the landing, the airplane impacted corn and uneven terrain, which resulted in a hard landing and main landing gear collapse. The airplane then nosed over and came to rest inverted. 

Initial examination of the wreckage by an FAA inspector revealed substantial damage to the wings, vertical stabilizer, and rudder. The wreckage was retained for further examination.

On June 30, 2026, at about 1030 eastern daylight time, an experimental Sonerai 2 airplane, N1406, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Cynthiana, Kentucky. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot reported that the purpose of the flight was to perform local air work in the traffic pattern. There were no anomalies noted during the preflight inspection, engine run-up, or subsequent takeoff. The airplane departed with 10 gallons of fuel. About 25 minutes into the flight, after completing two touch-and-go-landings, the airplane experienced a total loss of engine power while transitioning to the crosswind leg of the traffic pattern. The pilot was unable to restore engine power and performed a forced landing to a field west of the airport. During the landing roll, the landing gear separated and the fuselage impacted the ground resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage. 
Following the landing, the airplane’s lithium battery caught fire and consumed most of the fuselage. 
The wreckage was retained for further examination.

cause: The pilot’s improper fuel management, which resulted in fuel starvation and a loss of engine power.
t:
The pilot reported that, after flying most of the cross-country flight with the fuel selector set to the right fuel tank, he entered an extended downwind for landing at the destination airport. Just before turning base, the right fuel tank became empty and the engine stopped. He immediately turned the fuel selector to the left tank and attempted to restart the engine but was unsuccessful. He reported hearing the stall warning horn before the airplane “dropped out from under” him and impacted a dry riverbed, resulting in substantial damage to the fuselage and wings. 

The pilot reported that his improper fuel management resulted in fuel starvation and the subsequent loss of engine power. He further remarked that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The passenger’s abrupt manipulation of the flight controls during takeoff, which resulted in a loss of directional control and collision with a fence.
t: The flight instructor and the student pilot had just completed a training flight, but still needed to fly back to their home airport. A friend of the pilot sat in the back of the airplane during the training flight. The student pilot asked the instructor if his friend, who had no flight training experience other than a discovery flight, could sit up front for the return flight. The instructor agreed and provided clear instructions to the friend to not touch any of the flight controls during the flight. The friend was asked if he had any questions about the takeoff and he said he had none. During the takeoff roll, the instructor said the friend tapped the left brake with his foot, which resulted in a “slight bump” of the airplane. This motion scared the friend, who then panicked and grabbed the control yoke and pulled it all the way back while moving it to the left. The left wing briefly touched the ground and the friend repeatedly screamed, “I’m sorry!” The friend did not let go of the controls, and the instructor had to wrestle him and repeatedly tell him to let go and that he had the controls. The instructor said he needed both hands to try and overcome the force the friend had on the controls. The instructor was able to get the airplane’s wings level just before it collided with a fence, which resulted in substantial damage to the wings and fuselage. The friend told first responders that he was the one that crashed the airplane and that “it was all his fault.”

cause: The pilot’s improper flare which resulted in a hard landing and their subsequent loss control of during a go-around. Contributing to the accident was the flight instructor’s inadequate remedial action.
t:
The flight instructor and pilot receiving instruction were conducting touch-and-go takeoffs and landings in the airport traffic pattern to familiarize the pilot with a recently purchased airplane. The flight instructor reported that, on the final landing, the pilot pitched the nose of the airplane up too aggressively for the flare. As a result of the high nose up attitude the airplane stalled, landed hard, and bounced back into the air. The pilot applied full engine power; however, the airplane remained in a nose up attitude, yawed to right, and bounced a second time. Subsequently, the airplane exited the runway surface and the right wing collided with an airport sign, which resulted in substantial damage to the right wing.
According to the flight instructor, after the second bounced landing, he directed the pilot to reduce the throttle to idle. The flight instructor added that on his side of the airplane he did not have access to the throttle or brakes, only shared access to the center control stick.
The pilot receiving instruction reported that there were no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: An inadvertent collision with a large wave during touchdown on a river, which resulted in a subsequent bounce and hard landing.
t: The pilot of the amphibious airplane reported that he performed a go-around during the first approach to the river seaplane base as the water did not look good (choppy). The water looked good during the second approach and the airplane touched down smooth, but the pilot did not see a large wave off the left side due to flat light, and the left float contacted the wave. The contact resulted in the airplane bouncing up into the air and contacting the water a second time, resulting in a hard landing and collapsed left float strut. The hard landing also resulted in substantial damage to the left elevator. The pilot added that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The student pilot’s failure to maintain a proper glidepath, which resulted in a long landing and collision with a person on the ground.
t:
The student pilot reported that he extended the downwind leg to accommodate a departing tow airplane. During the subsequent approach, the glider was high. The pilot did not use the dive brakes to reduce altitude and attempted a forward slip; however, the glider remained high and fast throughout the approach. As a result, the glider touched down near the end and right side of the runway. During the subsequent landing rollout, the right wing struck a person on the ground, which resulted in serious injury. The glider then ground looped and sustained substantial damage to the right wing. 
The pilot reported no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the glider that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s failure to maintain control of the UAS during takeoff.
t:
The pilot/operator commanded the takeoff sequence on the agricultural unmanned aircraft system (UAS) and the UAS climbed to about 15 ft above its launch rig. Hearing an abnormal “popping” noise coming from the UAS, the pilot initiated the automated landing sequence and the UAS descended to about 2 ft above the rig and about 4 to 5 ft from the operator’s station. The pilot lost control of the UAS as it moved towards his position causing the pilot to duck behind the operator’s barrier. When he ducked, the UAS’s right-rear propeller struck his left hand resulting in a serious injury. The UAS descended and crashed into terrain resulting in substantial damage to the right-rear arm and propeller.
The operator sent the UAS on-board data to the manufacturer for decoding. The manufacturer’s report found that about 1 second after the UAS started up, a joystick input was received which paused the UAS’s takeoff. A couple seconds later, additional control inputs were recorded and the UAS responded accordingly. The data found no mechanical malfunction or failure with all engine parameters in the normal range.

cause: The flight instructor’s improper decision to leave the airplane with the engine running, which resulted in the airplane rolling forward and impacting a hangar.
t: The flight instructor stated that after the engine was started, he realized that the wheel chocks were still in place and not been removed from the left main landing gear. The flight instructor told the new student pilot to press the brake pedals with his feet while got out and removed the chocks. After the flight instructor climbed out of the airplane, it started to roll forward and impacted a hangar, resulting in substantial damage to the right wing’s leading edge. The flight instructor stated that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s failure to ensure that the landing gear were extended prior to landing.
t:
Before departing, the pilot found that the airplane’s battery was “low,” so he connected it to a charger for 15 minutes, after which he was able to start the engine normally. He subsequently completed three flight legs uneventfully, and was returning to his home airport when the accident occurred. As the pilot approached the destination airport, he noted that there was a thunderstorm in the area and elected to perform a downwind landing. During the landing approach, the pilot moved the landing gear position lever to the down position and extended the flaps. Due to the position the position of an electronic flight bag device in the cockpit, he did not observe that the landing gear down position indicator had not illuminated, nor did he realize that the landing gear circuit breaker had tripped. The pilot subsequently landed the airplane with the landing gear retracted, which resulted in substantial damage to the underside of the airplane’s fuselage.
Postaccident testing of the airplane’s landing gear revealed that it functioned normally when external electrical power was applied, and that the landing gear position indication lights operated normally. Functional testing of the airplane’s alternator and ammeter revealed that they functioned normally, but that the airplane’s battery had little to no capacity due to having dead cells. It is likely that the battery’s degraded condition resulted in the tripped landing gear system circuit breaker during the accident flight, and resulted in the landing gear’s failure to extend. Had the pilot noticed that the landing gear did not extend as expected, he could have taken additional troubleshooting steps rather than continuing the landing with the landing gear not extended.

Malta Air, doing business as Ryanair flight 1879, a Boeing 737-8AS, registration 9H-QEU, experienced a No. 2 (right) engine fan-blade-out (FBO) failure during climb out from the Thessaloniki International Airport (SKG), Thessaloniki, Greece. Engine fragments breached the fuselage and the cabin depressurized. The crew elected to return to SKG where they made an uneventful landing. The flight was a scheduled international passenger flight from SKG to Memmingen Airport (FMM), Memmingen, Germany. There were 2 pilots, 4 flight attendants, and 149 passengers (including one lap child) on board. One passenger sustained serious injuries.

The NTSB traveled to the accident site. On July 16, 2026, the Greece Hellenic Air and Railway Safety Investigation Authority (HARSIA) delegated the investigation in full to the NTSB. As part of the investigative process, the NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation. These included the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), The Boeing Company, and GE Aerospace. In accordance with the provisions of Annex 13 to the Convention on International Civil Aviation, the countries of Greece (State of Occurrence), Malta (State of the Operator and Registry), and France (State of Manufacture of the Engines, jointly with the United States) designated Accredited Representatives to the investigation, and Malta Air, Safran Aircraft Engines, and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) were designated as technical advisors. 

The parties were formed into specialized investigative groups led by NTSB group chairs in the areas of Powerplants, Structures and Survival Factors, and Materials Engineering. The Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) and Flight Data Recorder (FDR) were sent to NTSB headquarters for download and specialists were assigned. The materials engineer traveled to France to lead the engine fan blade examination. 

History of Flight
According to the flight crew, while climbing through an altitude of about 16,000 ft, near Polykastro, Greece, (about 4.5 nm south of the Greek border with Northern Macedonia) they received a No. 2 engine HIGH VIBRATION indication. They reduced the engine power and initiated the Engine High Vibration non-normal checklist. Shortly after, the engine vibration indication was reduced. The crew subsequently continued the climb on autopilot. 

The engine vibrations then increased significantly, they heard a loud bang, and the autopilot was disengaged. While assessing the engine condition, the cabin altitude warning sounded. The flight crew donned their oxygen masks, declared an emergency, and began an immediate descent. 

The flight attendants (FAs), who were preparing for cabin service, reported hearing and feeling a loud continuous vibration and seeing a small amount of fog/smoke before the oxygen masks dropped. One reported hearing an automated public address system announcement saying “emergency descent”. Another recalled manually making an additional decompression

On July 13, 2026, about 2236 eastern daylight time, a Smith Aerostar 601P, N800AA was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Lake Clear, New York. The private pilot and two passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.

According to preliminary information from the FAA, the airplane was based at Monmouth Executive Airport (BLM), Belmar, New Jersey. Earlier on the night of the accident, the pilot flew uneventfully from BLM to Adirondack Regional Airport (SLK), Saranac Lake, New York. He intended to pick up two family members and return to BLM the same evening. FAA ADS-B data were available for the inbound flight; however, the airplane did not gain enough altitude on the outbound flight for FAA ADS-B data to be recorded.

SLK was located at 1,662 ft above mean sea level (msl) and runway 23 was 6,573 ft-long. Review of third-party commercial surveillance data revealed that the accident flight departed runway 23, at 2235:45. The last target was recorded 46 seconds later, at 2236:31, indicating a location about 1 mile from the departure end of the runway. The data also indicated that the airplane reached a maximum height of about 125 ft above ground level (agl), before descending and leveling off at 75 ft agl for the last five recorded targets, spanning 12 seconds. During that time, the groundspeed increased from 151 knots to 169 knots. 

Review of home security video near the accident site revealed an engine sound at 2236, followed by the sound of collision with trees. The wreckage was located about 4 hours later by first responders, and a postimpact fire had consumed a majority of the airplane. 

A debris path was observed in a nearby forest, beginning with a section of right wingtip, located about 1-mile beyond the departure end of runway 23. The debris path extended on a 230° magnetic course for about 1/2 mile, to the main wreckage. Severed trees, a section of right flap, and a small section of lower empennage were also located along the debris path. The wreckage came to rest flat and upright, oriented on a magnetic heading of 180°, at an elevation about 1,668 ft msl. 

All major components of the airplane were identified. Both engines were located near the main wreckage and both propellers remained attached to their respective engine. The empennage was located next to the left engine, and sections of both wings were identified near the main wreckage. The cockpit and cabin were consumed by fire. 

The pilot held a private pilot certificate with ratings for airplane single engine land, airplane single-engine sea, airplane multiengine land, instrument airplane, and rotorcraft helicopter. He reported a total flight experience of 1,025 hours on an application for an FAA third-class medical certificate, dated December 17, 2025. The pilot obtained an instrument rating on October 3, 2024. At that time, he reported a total flight experience of 890 hours; of which,

cause: The pilot's failure to maintain clearance from an antenna while maneuvering during a low-level aerial application flight.
t:
The pilot reported that while making a low-level aerial application pass over a corn field, he heard a loud bang and felt as if the airplane impacted something. He attempted to increase the engine power, but the engine did not respond to the throttle control inputs. The pilot performed an emergency hopper dump of the liquid chemical load and conducted a forced landing to a flat grass field, and a post-impact fire ensued.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, engine mount, elevator, and both wings. The propeller hub was found near a damaged antenna about .75 mi from where the airplane came to rest. The antenna was located inside of a metal fence, next to a small white building. The pilot reported that there were no pre-impact malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s inability to see and avoid a piece of loose wire in a field during an off-airport landing in a glider, which resulted in a ground loop. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s inability to maintain a safe position behind the tow airplane after taking off which required them to release from tow at too low of an altitude to return to the airport.
t: The pilot reported that he was piloting a glider while being towed by a tow airplane. Shortly after takeoff, and during a turn, the glider lost safe positioning behind the tow airplane and climbed above it due to a possible wind gust. The pilot deemed he would not be able to recover to a safe position and released the tow rope about 300 ft AGL. The pilot determined he could not make a turn back to the airport and elected to conduct an off-airport landing on a nearby field. During the landing a wingtip caught a section of loose wire that was hidden in tall grass in the field, which resulted in a ground loop. The tail boom fractured, resulting in substantial damage to the glider. The pilot reported there were no pre-impact mechanical anomalies that contributed to the accident.

cause: Degraded engine and propeller performance during hot and high-density altitude operations, which resulted in a high descent rate and subsequent hard landing.
t:
On June 26, 2026, about 1140 Pacific daylight time, an experimental Leigh Aerosystems E100 unmanned aircraft system (UAS) experienced a hard landing at Bisbee Douglas International Airport, Douglas, Arizona. At the time of the accident, the aircraft was operated by a remote pilot as a flight test under the provisions of Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 and a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Certificate of Authorization (COA). The aircraft sustained substantial damage and there were no injuries to ground personnel. 

Figure 1. Leigh Aerosystems E100 UAS. (Source: Northrop Grumman)
According to the remote pilot, the intent of the flight was to test the aircraft’s hover capabilities and develop performance data for hot day conditions. The aircraft performed controlled flight up to a planned altitude of about 40 ft above ground level but then began to descend at a rate faster than planned. The aircraft subsequently experienced a hard landing about 10-15 ft from its takeoff location, resulting in the right spar and wing separating from the fuselage. The aircraft was subsequently shut down. Postaccident analysis by the operator of the flight test found that the high-density altitude (about 7,500 ft) at the time of the flight degraded both engine and propeller performance, which limited the maneuverability and controllability of the aircraft.

cause: An encounter with convectively induced turbulence during cruise flight in an area of forecast thunderstorm activity.
t:
On July 16, 2026, about 1502 eastern daylight time, SkyWest Airlines, operating as Delta Connection flight 3723, encountered severe turbulence while in cruise flight at FL370 en route to Hartsfield/Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Atlanta, Georgia. Of the 71 passengers and crew members aboard, one flight attendant sustained a serious injury. The flight was operating under 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 121 as a regularly scheduled international passenger flight from North Eleuthera Airport (ELH), North Eleuthera, Bahamas, to ATL.
According to the flight crew, after departure they received an instrument flight rules (IFR) clearance to ATL with an initial climb to FL230, followed by FL340. During the climb, they encountered light turbulence associated with nearby cloud tops and requested a higher altitude to improve ride quality. The flight was subsequently cleared to FL360. After turning northbound, air traffic control (ATC) asked if they would prefer FL350 or FL370; the crew accepted FL370. The flight then continued in smooth air for about 50 minutes.
As the flight progressed, the flight crew observed cumulonimbus clouds along the route of flight and requested a deviation to the right. Flight attendants (FA) were advised of the potential for turbulence and told to use caution. While the fasten seat belt sign remained illuminated. ATC was unable to approve the request but authorized a deviation to the left. After completing the deviation, the flight was cleared direct SHRKS.
About 6 minutes later, the airplane encountered severe turbulence that lasted approximately 5 seconds. The flight crew reported no visual indications of impending turbulence from the flight deck and no corresponding returns on the onboard weather radar. During the encounter, the airplane experienced a loss of airspeed and activation of the stick shaker. The captain called "upset" and initiated recovery procedures. The airplane lost about 300 to 400 ft before recovery was completed and cruise flight at FL370 was resumed. 
At the time of the turbulence encounter, the forward flight attendant was in the forward galley after completing cabin service. During the turbulence encounter, she braced herself and then took her jumpseat. Following the encounter, passengers requested assistance after observing the aft flight attendant lying on the rear galley floor, having reportedly struck her head during the turbulence encounter. The forward flight attendant solicited assistance from medically qualified passengers, who evaluated and assisted the injured flight attendant. She subsequently notified the flight crew of the injury and checked for additional passenger injuries.
After receiving notification of the injury, the flight crew coordinated with company dispatch and diverted to Jacksonville International Airport (JAX), Jacksonville, Florida, where emergency medical services met the airplane upon arrival. The FA was subsequently transported to a hospital and was

cause: The pilot’s inadequate lookout, which resulted in a collision with ground equipment during taxi.
t:
The pilot reported that he performed four practice landings at the departure airport, to confirm landing performance, then continued to a private gravel airstrip. He overflew the airstrip and observed calm wind conditions, then performed another flyover to verify the runway was clear of obstructions. While on final approach, a gust of wind resulted in a temporary increase in airspeed then a touchdown farther than planned. After landing, during a “fast-taxi maneuver” he struck ground equipment that was obscured because of the tailwheel airplane’s nose-high pitch attitude. The landing gear collapsed, then the airplane then struck another piece of equipment, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing. 
The pilot stated that there were no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures of the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s failure to extend the landing gear before landing.
t:
The pilot reported that while he was on approach, a communication with the air traffic control (ATC) tower controller interrupted his completion of the before landing checklist. The pilot reported that he forgot to resume the checklist and lower the landing gear. About 20 ft above the runway, the ATC controller alerted the pilot that his landing gear was retracted. The pilot applied full engine power and attempted to lower the landing gear; however, the airplane touched down on the runway without the landing gear properly configured, which resulted in substantial damage to the left wing and left aileron. 
The pilot did not submit the National Transportation Safety Board Pilot/Operator Aircraft Accident/Incident Report Form 6120.1.

cause: The pilot’s failure to maintain control of the airplane during takeoff, resulting in an aerodynamic stall and impact with water.
t: The pilot of the amphibious airplane reported that he was attempting to take off from a glassy water surface. The pilot had trouble getting the airplane “unstuck” from the water surface, so he pulled back on the control stick “extra hard.” This action broke the floats free from the surface tension but created a nose-high pitch attitude that resulted in the airplane entering an aerodynamic stall. The left float then impacted the water and it broke loose from the airplane before striking the underside of the left wing, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing. The airplane came to rest upright but slowly began to sink. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during landing with a right crosswind, which resulted in the airplane’s impact with terrain.
t:
The pilot reported that while attempting to land, the airplane touched down, encountered a right crosswind, and began to drift to the left. The pilot attempted to correct the movement by applying opposite rudder and subsequently increased engine power to attempt to go around. However, the left wing contacted the ground, and the airplane then impacted terrain. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right wing, tail and empennage. 
The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical failures or malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

On July 27, 2026, about 2130 Alaska daylight time, a deregistered Piper PA-22-150 airplane, N4535A, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Chitina, Alaska. The pilot and two passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
According to witnesses, the pilot and two passengers departed McCarthy Airport, McCarthy, Alaska, to drop off the passengers and supplies at the upper Dan Creek airstrip, located about 12 miles southeast of McCarthy. The upper Dan Creek airstrip is an uncharted private strip that is generally considered one way in and out, surrounded by steeply rising terrain, and go-arounds are not recommended.
Multiple witnesses, located on the ground in the vicinity of the airstrip, reported hearing the airplane approaching the southeast runway for landing at a normal approach power setting. The witnesses stated that they then heard the airplane’s engine increase to a high-power setting, then there was a moment of silence, followed by the sound of an impact.

The airplane impacted a berm on a rock-covered riverbank in a left-wing-low flight attitude about 740 ft north of the airstrip. The wreckage was oriented on a northwest heading. All four corners of the airplane were accounted for at the accident site. The outboard portion of the left wing was bent downwards and aft. The fuselage, inboard left wing, and portions of the inboard right wing were consumed by a postimpact fire.
During the onsite investigation, no preimpact anomalies were visually observed with the flight control system. The fuel selector was positioned on the left tank, and 100LL aviation fuel was present in the left wing. The throttle was found in the idle position and was bent in the direction of the pilot. The propeller blades exhibited rotational signatures including leading edge tip damage and chordwise witness marks, indicative of operation at a low-power setting upon impact.
The engine has been recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

cause: The pilot’s inadvertent selection of the fuel selector valve to the OFF position resulted in a total loss of engine power due to fuel starvation and subsequent forced landing to a field.
t:
The pilot of the tailwheel equipped airplane reported that he was preparing the airplane for landing and the landing gear would not extend. He attempted to extend the landing gear using the airplane’s manual gear extension procedure and during that effort, the fuel selector valve was inadvertently moved to the OFF position rather than the hydraulic system depressurization valve. The engine experienced a total loss of power, and the pilot initiated a forced landing to a field, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing and fuselage. 
The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The flight instructor and pilot receiving instruction’s failure to verify that the landing gear was extended before landing, which resulted in a gear-up landing.
t:
The flight instructor reported that at some point between the base turn and final approach, the landing gear selector switch was inadvertently moved to the UP or gear retracted position. Unknown to the flight instructor or the pilot receiving instruction, the airplane subsequently landed with the landing gear retracted and sustained substantial damage to the lower fuselage. 
Postaccident examination of the landing gear selector switch revealed that the safety notch was worn and allowed the switch to move from the DOWN position to the UP position with minimal force. The worn condition of the safety notch could have increased the likelihood of an inadvertent movement of the selector switch during flight.

On August 6, 2026, about 1030 central daylight time, a Beech H35, N5409D, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Bogalusa, Louisiana. The private pilot and passenger were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
Preliminary ADS-B data showed the airplane departed Elm Creek Airpark (0TX6), Seguin, Texas, where the airplane was based, at 0617. The airplane arrived at George R Carr Memorial Air Field (BXA), Bogalusa, Louisiana, about 0915. According to the airport manager at BXA, the pilot wanted 40 gallons of fuel. He continued that the pilot “topped off” the left and right main fuel tanks and was adding fuel to the right auxiliary fuel tank when the fuel farm pump motor stopped working. The pilot had added 35 gallons at that point and told the airport manager that this would be enough fuel. 
The airport manager also reported that the pilot had wanted to put more fuel into the right side of the airplane to help “get the plane trimmed better.” The airport manager asked the pilot if he planned to use the crew vehicle to go into town to get something to eat, the pilot told him no, that they had left early and were on their way to Florida. Motion-activated surveillance cameras at the airport showed the pilot and passenger in the fixed base operator (FBO) building and the airport manager reported that he spoke with the pilot about the next leg of their flight to Florida. The pilot told him that they would stop on their way back to Texas the following Tuesday. The airport manager then left to begin working on the fuel farm pump and the cameras show the pilot and passenger leaving the FBO at 1013. The cameras that were pointed at the ramp did not capture any other footage of the pilot and passenger, or the accident airplane. The airport manager continued that while at the fuel farm working on the pump he saw the pilot doing a walkaround but did not watch the full preflight inspection and was not sure if the pilot sumped the airplane’s fuel tanks. He then heard the pilot start the engine, which took two tries before it started. He watched as the airplane taxied out to the runway and heard the pilot perform an engine run-up. He then watched the takeoff roll, rotation, and initial climb before he turned and began putting tools away. When he exited the fuel farm pit and began to place his tools in his truck, he saw a smoke plume and went to the accident site where he found the airplane consumed by a postimpact fire. He did not report hearing any abnormalities in the engine noise during the engine run-up or takeoff/initial climb.
The accident site was located about 0.5 statute miles from the departure end of runway 36, the runway the airplane departed from, in a forested area. A pine tree about 10 ft aft and outboard of the right wing tip had two branches broken about 40 ft up the tree with the higher branch broken closer to the trunk. A large log was embedded in the cowling

cause: The pilot’s failure to ensure the canopy was properly locked before flight, which resulted in the canopy opening during takeoff.
t: The pilot reported that while completing his preflight checks of the airplane, he thought that he had closed and locked its canopy, though he did not push up after locking it as was his usual habit. Shortly after starting the takeoff roll for a local flight, the canopy opened and struck the airplane’s right wing, substantially damaging the canopy. The pilot immediately aborted the takeoff and taxied back to the ramp without further incident. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

On August 5, 2026, at about 1034 mountain daylight time, a Van’s Aircraft RV-8, C-GFWR, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Great Falls, Montana. The pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The airplane departed Villeneuve Airport (CZVL), near Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, and landed on runway 21 at Great Falls International Airport (KGTF), Great Falls, Montana. During the landing rollout, the airplane veered right. The pilot applied engine power while attempting to regain directional control, and the airplane subsequently ground looped to the right and departed the runway. The left main landing gear collapsed, and the left wing contacted the ground. The airplane came to rest in the grass adjacent to the runway.
The airplane sustained substantial damage to the left wing, and fuselage. The pilot reported that the tailwheel assembly had been replaced about two weeks before the accident and that the accident flight was the airplane’s first flight and landing since the replacement.
The airplane was retained for examination.

On August 15, 2026, 1755 Alaska Daylight Time, a China Airlines Flight Number CI-5265, Boeing 747-400F, registration B-18725, powered by four GE Aerospace CF6-80C2B1F turbofan engines, experienced an inflight fire indication during the initial climb from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (PANC). There were no injuries to the 4 crewmembers, and the airplane sustained minor damage. The flight was an international cargo flight from ANC to Taoyuan International Airport (RCTP), Taiwan.

According to the pilot, after takeoff at about 5,500ft above mean sea level (MSL), there was an audible fire warning and an "ENG FIRE 3" Engine-Indicating and Crew-Alerting System (EICAS) warning indication illuminated. The crew discharged one fire extinguishing bottle and shutdown the No. 3 engine. During the inflight shutdown procedure, electrical AC Bus Tie 3 tripped and electrical AC Bus 3 de-energized, which resulted in the left-hand autopilot disengaging and the loss of multiple instruments on the captain’s side. The crew engaged the Center autopilot and declared Mayday with air traffic control (ATC). ATC vectored the airplane to a holding pattern to jettison fuel prior to landing, but the fuel jettison control system failed. With the No. 3 engine fire warning no longer illuminated following discharge of the fire extinguishing bottle, the airplane remained in a holding pattern to burn enough fuel to be under the overweight landing limits at PANC. The airplane landed uneventfully approximately two hours after takeoff.

A post incident examination of the airplane by maintenance personnel revealed fire damage to a lower section of the left-hand engine cowl and evidence of an undercowl fire on the left-hand side of the engine. 

The NTSB traveled to the incident site. As part of the investigative process, the NTSB invited qualified parties to participate in the investigation. These included representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), GE Aerospace, and Boeing. The Taiwan Transportation Safety Board (TTSB), representing the State of the Operator, assigned an Accredited Representative; the Civil Aviation Administration (CAA) of Taiwan and China Airlines were named as a technical advisor by the TTSB. The investigation team traveled to ANC to examine the airplane. A pressurization check of the fuel manifolds with nitrogen gas revealed a crack in the left-hand (inboard) fuel manifold tube, located adjacent to fuel nozzle number 24 at approximately the 9 o’clock position on the engine. The engine was later removed from the airplane and shipped to an engine repair and overhaul facility for further examination. 

This investigation is ongoing..

cause: The pilot's failure to maintain clearance from power lines while maneuvering at low-level altitude during an agricultural operation.
t:
The pilot reported he was conducting aerial pollination in a corn field. Before beginning the pollination, the pilot flew an inspection circuit around the area to identify potential hazards and observed a center-pivot irrigation system and the power lines along the east and west sides of the field. The pilot reported that he completed about 3/4 of the field pollination and had two passes remaining. While turning the helicopter to enter another pass, the pilot focused on the target row, lost sight of the power lines, and the helicopter struck a power line wire with the tail rotor. 
Following the wire strike, the pilot elected to perform a precautionary landing. During the landing, the helicopter contacted the ground on the right skid, bounced, and yawed slightly to the right before it came to a stop. 
A post-accident examination of the helicopter revealed substantial damage to the right rear aft strut mounting area, and damage to the pilot seat floor structure at the forward strut attachment. The pilot reported that there was no evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the helicopter that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s failure to maintain control of the airplane during an aborted landing, which resulted in a nose over on the grass runway.
t: The pilot of the tailwheel-equipped airplane reported that while attempting a three-point landing on a grass airstrip, the airplane bounced twice. After the second bounce, the pilot increased engine power and was attempting to abort the landing when he lost control of the airplane. It subsequently nosed over and came to rest inverted on the runway, resulting in substantial damage to the left wing and vertical stabilizer. The pilot did not report that there were any preimpact mechanical malfunctions with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s failure to properly stow the motor in preparation for approach and landing that resulted in a loss of airspeed and an inadvertent aerodynamic stall and spin.
t:
The pilot of the electric motor glider stated that in preparation for decent and landing to the destination airport, he selected the system enable switch to off instead of selecting the motor mast position selector to down. The motor then windmilled, which resulted in the motor and mast losing power, and the glider quickly lost airspeed. The glider then entered an aerodynamic stall and spin. The pilot stated that in an attempt to recover from the spin, he pushed down on the control stick and applied rudder, but the glider pitched up violently. While in an unusual attitude and at a low altitude, the pilot was unable to regain control and deployed the ballistic parachute. During the deployment, the parachute rocket went through the right wing, but the parachute still deployed and the glider impacted terrain in an inverted attitude. The glider sustained substantial damage to the right wing. 
The pilot attributed the rapid loss of the glider’s airspeed due to the drag induced from the windmilling propeller and thought that the windmilling propeller also inhibited airflow over the vertical and horizontal stabilizer, which prevented recovery from the stall and spin. The pilot stated there was no mechanical malfunctions or failures with the glider that precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s failure to extend the landing gear before landing.
t:
The pilot reported that while on final approach, he believed he had lowered the landing gear. He stated that during the landing, the touchdown was light and he did not realize there was an issue until he heard the lower fuselage grinding against the asphalt runway. He stated that the accident could have been prevented by confirming that the landing gear was extended and locked on short final. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the lower fuselage.
The pilot reported no preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures with the airplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The pilot’s improper execution of rejected takeoff procedures, which resulted in loss of control and subsequent runway excursion.
t: During the takeoff roll from the 600 ft grass airstrip, the gyroplane hit a large bump which caused the glove box to open, and its contents fall into the cockpit. He believed there was enough runway remaining and attempted to reject the takeoff. During the rejected takeoff, the pilot inadvertently applied the throttle handle instead of the handbrake. The gyroplane continued off the end of the runway and into a pond, which resulted in substantial damage to the empennage and a main rotor blade. The pilot reported that there were no preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures with the gyroplane that would have precluded normal operation.

cause: The misfuelling of the airplane by the refueler. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s failure to verify that the airplane had been properly fueled prior to departing on the accident flight.
t:
The pilot of the reciprocating, multi-engine airplane reported that, after takeoff while climbing to altitude, the #1 cylinder on the right engine was running hot. He leveled the airplane at 5,000 mean sea level (msl), but the cylinder continued to run hot, so he elected to feather the propeller and shut down the engine. As he attempted to navigate to an airport, he noticed that the other engine was beginning to deteriorate and he was no longer able to maintain altitude. He attempted to increase power on the remaining engine but about 2 miles from the airport he performed a forced landing to a cornfield. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the right engine mount, fuselage, and empennage as a result.
A first responder on scene sampled fuel from one of the airplane’s fuel tanks with a paper towel and reported that the fuel did not have any color to it. She also reported that the fuel smelled like diesel fuel. A postaccident interview with the fueler at the departure airport confirmed that he had topped off the airplane with “pre-mixed Jet-A.” The airport manager at the departure airport confirmed that the fueler used Jet-A fuel when filling the airplane. A fuel receipt was provided by the airport manager, and was signed by the pilot, that showed the airplane had been fueled with 145 gallons of Jet-A.
In an interview with the pilot, he reported that he did not specifically tell the fueler that he wanted 100LL in the airplane. He also stated that he did read the fuel receipt after fueling and that they “wanted to get home” so they “got in the airplane and left.” The pilot did not inspect or sample fuel from the airplane’s tanks after the fuel was added.

On September 10, 2026, about 1005 mountain daylight time, a Cessna 210, N9517T, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Polson Airport (8S1), Polson, Montana. The student pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight
The pilot reported that he was returning to 8S1 after a short flight. The flight was uneventful until the airplane was on final approach. According to the pilot, the airplane was high on the approach, and he initiated a forward slip to increase the descent rate. About 20 to 30 seconds after entering the slip, the engine lost all power. The propeller continued to windmill during the descent The pilot verified the mixture and fuel selector positions and manipulated the throttle; however, he was unsuccessful in his attempt to restore engine power.
The pilot discontinued the slip and established a glide toward the airport. The airplane crossed a road near the approach end of the runway and struck a fence before coming to rest on the airport grass. The lower fuselage and left wing were substantially damaged during the accident sequence. The pilot reported that each wing tank contained about 16 gallons of fuel before departure.
Fuel samples were obtained from the airplane, and the airplane was retained for further examination.

On September 11, 2026 about 0830 eastern daylight time, a Robinson R44 helicopter, N4026E, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Colquitt, Georgia. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 agricultural flight.
According to the pilot, he completed a preflight inspection and engine run-up of the helicopter and found no anomalies. He verified all gauges were in the green and hovered the helicopter over to a trailer and landed on the trailer. Ground personnel added five gallons of fuel and loaded 50 lbs of liquid to the helicopter while the helicopter remained running. The ground personnel unhooked all the hoses from the helicopter and gave the pilot a signal it was safe to depart from the trailer. The pilot lifted the helicopter to a hover over the trailer and verified all gauges were still in the green. The pilot pushed forward on the cyclic to depart from the trailer, as the helicopter began to move forward, he felt a jolt and heard and felt the engine “skipping.” Subsequently the engine lost partial power and the helicopter settled into the terrain resulting in a hard landing. The helicopter sustained substantial damage to the tail boom, tail rotor gear box, and tail rotor blades. 
A detailed wreckage examination is pending.

On September 17, 2026, about 0720 eastern daylight time, a Weatherly Aviation Company Inc. 602B, N20003, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Lynchburg, South Carolina. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 aerial application flight. 
According to a family member, the pilot departed a private airstrip in Woodrow, South Carolina and flew to a private airstrip in Oswego, South Carolina. The airplane was loaded with about 20 gallons of herbicide, which was to be applied on a nearby corn field. The flight was planned to take about 30 to 45 minutes. According to the landowner, he received a phone call from a family member of the pilot asking if the pilot had completed the job. The landowner subsequently saw smoke in the vicinity of the corn field and found the airplane inverted and on fire. 
The accident site was located about 10 miles east of the departure location. The airplane impacted the ground on magnetic heading of 134o, at an elevation of 154 ft mean sea level (msl). The debris field measured 300 ft by 180 ft with all major components of the airplane located within the debris field. The right wing was impact separated and located 96 ft from the initial ground impact with the right main landing gear assembly still attached. The leading edge of the right wing was crushed aft with engine oil on the wing surface. The fuselage, left wing, and empennage came to rest on a magnetic heading of 255o. The fuselage was partially consumed by a postaccident fire from the cockpit forward. The left wing was partially attached to the fuselage with thermal damage at the wing root and the leading edge crushed aft. The empennage remained attached to the fuselage with the left elevator crushed. The rudder was impact separated and was found near the engine about 20 ft from the fuselage. The rudder exhibited thermal damage to the lower rudder cap. 
The engine, engine mount, and firewall were separated and came to rest about 20 ft from the fuselage. Engine cylinder Nos. 3, 4, and 5 exhibited impact damage to the cylinder head assemblies. The No. 2-cylinder head was fractured. It did not display impact damage and was found within the debris field. The accessory section of the engine, the firewall, and engine mount exhibited thermal damage. 
The wreckage was retained for further examination.

On September 29, 2026, about 1828 central daylight time, a Cessna 152 II airplane, N69009, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Bolingbrook, Illinois. The flight instructor and the student pilot sustained minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
The purpose of the local area flight was for the flight instructor to provide instruction to the student pilot, as part of JWA Flight School. JWA Flight School is based at the Bolingbrook’s Clow International Airport (1C5), Bolingbrook, Illinois.
The airplane had a preflight inspection performed by both the flight instructor and the student pilot, and no abnormalities were noted. The student pilot was stationed in the left front seat, and the flight instructor was stationed in the right front seat. The airplane had about 24.5 gallons of 100 low lead fuel onboard for the flight.
The engine runup process was completed and no abnormalities were noted. During the initial climb from runway 18 at 1C5, the student pilot who was manipulating the flight controls noted that “something was not right.” The flight instructor then immediately assumed the flight controls. She observed the tachometer and noticed that the engine RPM had decreased to about 20 RPM. She then executed the emergency procedure checklist and realized the airplane did not have sufficient engine power to climb due to the partial power loss, and the airplane was losing altitude. She performed a forced landing to a flat grass sports field in a residential area, about 0.25 miles southwest of the departure end of runway 18.
The airplane came to rest upright in a nose-down profile on the grass field. During the impact sequence, the empennage separated about midspan. The student pilot was able to egress from the airplane on his own accord; however, the flight instructor was removed from the airplane by a bystander. The airplane sustained substantial damage to the fuselage, both wings, and the empennage. The airplane was recovered from the accident site and transported to a secure location for future examination.
The airplane was manufactured in 1978. The airplane was equipped with a Lycoming Engines O-235-L2C reciprocating engine and a McCauley Propeller 1A103/TCM6958 fixed-pitch two-blade aluminum propeller.
A review of the airplane’s maintenance records showed that an annual inspection was performed by a mechanic on July 23, 2026, for the airframe, the engine, and the propeller. Since the annual inspection occurred, the airplane had accumulated 40.9 hours. At the time of the accident, the airplane had accumulated a total of 14,851.9 hours.
The flight instructor completed a flight review on April 24, 2025.

On October 12, 2026, at 1540 central daylight time, a Piper PA-28-140 airplane, N9859W, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Abita Springs, Louisiana. The private pilot was uninjured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight.
The pilot stated that he topped off the airplane fuel level for a personal flight that was to remain in the local area. He stated the engine runup for the flight was performed with a left fuel tank selection, the runup was normal, and he did not change fuel tank positions for the duration of the flight. He then performed two full stop takeoff and landings without incident prior to attempting a third takeoff. During the third takeoff roll and rotation, the engine instrument indications were normal. While the airplane climbed through 700 ft above ground level and entered a left turn for the downwind leg of the airport traffic pattern, the engine “sputtered.” The pilot stated that he verified the mixture control was in the full rich position and the fuel pump was on and “checked the carburetor heat with no apparent effect.” Shortly afterwards, the airplane experienced a total loss of engine power. The pilot stated that he engaged the engine starter, heard the starter operate, and saw the propeller turn, but the engine did not restart. He initially turned the airplane toward the departure runway but determined that the airplane would not have sufficient altitude to clear the trees along the return course. He identified an open field to his right, with a dirt road running through it, and selected that area for landing. During landing, the airplane impacted terrain and sustained substantial damage to the airplane’s left wing.
The airplane owner stated that the airplane had not received a current annual inspection under CFR Part 91.409 at the time of the accident.
The airplane was retained for further examination.

On October 15, 2026 at 1330 eastern daylight time, a Hughes 269C, N9655F, sustained substantial damage when it was involved in an accident near Gastonia, North Carolina. The pilot was not injured. The helicopter was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight.
The student pilot reported that he was practicing solo traffic pattern operations at Gastonia Municipal Airport (AKH), Gastonia, Georgia. Before touchdown on the fourth landing, less than 100 ft above ground level and less than 45 knots indicated airspeed, the pilot heard a loud bang. Immediately after, he heard the engine rpm increase and the rotor rpm decrease.
The pilot continued and landed the helicopter hard on the runway. He reported that the helicopter’s tail struck the ground, but that the helicopter landed upright on its skids. After exiting the helicopter, he observed that the clutch linear actuator was broken. 
A post-accident examination conducted by an FAA inspector revealed that the actuating shaft for the clutch linear actuator was fractured, and the cable that connected it to the helicopter’s clutch assembly was no longer under tension. Substantial damage was observed to the helicopter’s fuselage and tail rotor transmission.
The wreckage was recovered and retained for further examination.
